extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of formal logic and philosophy (advanced undergraduates, graduate students, philosophers)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for recognizing, classifying, and evaluating inferences (syllogistic and inductive), including when apparent inferences are not real, how definitions function in proofs, and formal requirements for valid syllogisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions vs. assertions about things
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions are properly of names only, not of things; assertions that appear as premises when stated as definitions do not themselves establish facts about real objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A definition supplies a proposition relating to meaning (verbal), not a factual claim about existing objects. If a definition is treated as if it asserts the real existence of an object, a tacit postulate of existence is being smuggled in. Example: treating 'A dragon is a thing which breathes flame' as implying dragons exist is to assume a matter of fact not contained in the definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitute 'means' for 'is' to avoid tacit existence assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: When premises are definitions, replace 'is' with 'means' to avoid the tacit assumption of real existence and to make explicit that the proposition is about meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: change 'A dragon is a thing which breathes flame' to 'Dragon is a word meaning a thing which breathes flame.' From such verbal premises the only correct conclusion is about meanings (Some words which mean a serpent also mean a thing which breathes flame), not about existent things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish verbal (definitional) propositions from real propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions respecting the meaning of words (including definitions) are verbal and not susceptible to truth or falsity in the way real propositions are; assertions respecting things (real propositions) are appropriate subjects of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a proposition concerns meanings or matters of fact. Only real propositions (about existence, order, causation, resemblance) admit proof or disproof; definitions do not prove factual claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultimate categories of what propositions assert
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever their form, real propositions ultimately assert facts of one or more of: Existence, Order in Place, Order in Time, Causation, or Resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to analyze the import of propositions and to decide what kind of evidence or proof is appropriate for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for genuine inference (conclusion must add new content)
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine inference is one in which the conclusion is genuinely distinct from the premises; cases where the conclusion merely repeats or reformulates what was already asserted are not real inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the conclusion contains new information not already contained (explicitly or implicitly) in the premises. Examples of non-inference: converting universal to particular (All A is B → Some A is B) or asserting connoted attributes again (Socrates is a man → Socrates is a living creature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion and equipollency are not necessarily inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes that convert propositions (turning predicate into subject and vice versa) or show equipollency often only restate the same content in different words and therefore do not constitute real proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish simple verbal equivalence from inferential support. Conversion per accidens (All A is B → Some B is A), simple conversion (Some A is B → Some B is A), and conversion of universal negatives (No A is B → No B is A) are permitted transformations but may not add proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion of particular negatives via contraposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A particular negative (Some A is not B) can be converted by first rephrasing it as 'Some A is a thing which is not B' (a particular affirmative) and then converting that (Some thing not-B is A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that conversion of particular negatives requires changing the predicate to its complement (a thing which is not B) before applying simple conversion; otherwise no valid inversion follows (Some A is not B does not imply Some B is not A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical training: detect identity under verbal diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: An essential intellectual habit is the ability to recognize the identity of an assertion when it appears under different linguistic forms; this skill properly falls within the art of logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice conversion, opposition, and paraphrase to cultivate rapid and sure discernment of when two formulations assert the same content; this underpins sound interpretation and prevents treating paraphrases as distinct proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of proof (inference grounds belief)
rubrics_metrics.description: A fact or statement is proved when we believe it by reason of some other fact or statement from which it is said to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof requires that the alleged antecedent(s) genuinely provide grounds for accepting the conclusion; mere paraphrase or repetition does not constitute proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between apparent and proper cases of inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Several forms commonly presented as examples of syllogistic reasoning are only apparent inferences (equipollency, conversion, extracting particulars from universals, re-assertion of connoted attributes) and should be excluded from the province of reasoning properly so called.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an argument, check whether the 'inference' simply restates content already implicit in the premises; if so, treat it as paraphrase rather than proof. Textbooks for beginners often overuse such trivial examples, but logical education should emphasize substantive inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification: Induction vs. Ratiocination (generality test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction infers a proposition from premises less general than itself (conclusion more general than premises); Ratiocination (syllogism) infers a proposition from premises equally or more general (conclusion equally general or less general).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the relative generality of conclusion vs. premises to classify the type of reasoning. Induction collects a law from particulars (conclusion covers more than observed instances) and so is a real inferential enlargement; ratiocination derives conclusions within the same or narrower generality from general premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction as real inference (condition of legitimacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: In every induction the conclusion embraces more than is contained in the premises; induction is thus a real process of inference, and its legitimacy depends on conditions to be discussed (e.g., adequacy of observed instances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing an inductive inference, verify that the sample and method justify generalizing beyond observed cases; recognize induction as the process by which we infer future or unobserved facts from observed instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential formal requirements of a legitimate syllogism
rubrics_metrics.description: A legitimate syllogism must have exactly three propositions (two premises and a conclusion) and exactly three terms (major, minor, and middle); the middle term must occur in both premises; the major term is the predicate of the conclusion and occurs with the middle term in the major premise; the minor term is the subject of the conclusion and occurs with the middle term in the minor premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check syllogistic form for the three-term, three-proposition structure and correct placement of terms. Violations (extra terms, missing middle term, incorrect assignment of major/minor) render the syllogism illegitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures and moods of the syllogism (classification by middle term position and proposition quantity/quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllogisms are classified into figures according to the position of the middle term (subject/predicate pattern across premises) — first figure: middle term subject of major and predicate of minor (commonly); second figure: middle term predicate in both premises; third: subject in both; fourth: middle term subject of minor and predicate of major. Each figure is further divided into moods according to the quantity (universal/particular) and quality (affirmative/negative) of the propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or constructing syllogisms, determine figure by middle-term positions and check which moods (combinations of A/E/I/O forms) are legitimate within that figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: On the use of idealized postulates in demonstrative sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrative sciences often employ postulates that are not exactly true in reality (e.g., a circle with radii exactly equal), but as much of the postulate is true as is required to support as much of the conclusion as is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating deductive demonstrations that rely on idealized definitions, check that the portion of the idealization postulated actually supports the asserted part of the conclusion; apparent paradoxes from idealization do not invalidate proof if the necessary portion of the postulate holds for the case considered.
